title: Design messaging, event-driven and API architectures
learningObjective: Recommend a messaging architecture, an event-driven architecture and an API integration solution.
foundation: Parts of an app talk in two ways. A message is a request someone must handle (process this order). An event is news that something happened (a file was uploaded).
Queues and Service Bus carry messages; Event Grid and Event Hubs carry events. API Management puts a safe, managed front door on your APIs.
engineer: Messaging: Azure Queue Storage (simple, very large queues over 80 GB, at-least-once delivery, no ordering guarantees) and Azure Service Bus (enterprise broker: queues and topics with subscriptions and filters, FIFO through sessions, duplicate detection, dead-lettering, transactions, scheduled messages; Premium tier for VNet isolation, predictable performance and messages up to 100 MB). Patterns: competing consumers, queue-based load levelling, publish-subscribe.

Events: Event Grid (discrete events, push delivery to handlers, filtering, retries and dead-lettering; system topics for Azure resources, custom topics, namespaces with MQTT); Event Hubs (high-throughput event streaming with partitions, consumer groups, retention, Capture to storage and a Kafka endpoint). Event-driven styles: simple event processing (Event Grid → Function), stream processing (Event Hubs → Stream Analytics/Databricks), event sourcing.

APIs: Azure API Management (gateway with policies for authentication, rate limiting, caching and transformation; products and subscriptions; versions and revisions; developer portal; tiers from Consumption to Premium v2, with self-hosted gateways for hybrid). Combine with Application Gateway or Front Door for WAF, and private endpoints or VNet injection for internal APIs.

example.title: Order processing at an online retailer
body: Orders go onto a Service Bus topic; billing, shipping and email services each have a subscription with filters, and sessions keep each customer's orders in sequence.
Storage uploads raise Event Grid events to functions; clickstream data flows through Event Hubs to analytics; partners call order APIs through API Management with keys and rate limits.

prerequisites: An Azure subscription; most design reviews need only Reader access
permissions: Reader to review existing resources; Contributor or Owner to build the design
limits: Check service limits and regional availability for each component
portal: Service Bus namespace > Topics > Subscriptions and filters; queue properties (sessions, duplicate detection).
Event Grid > System topics / Event subscriptions.
API Management > APIs, Products, Policies, Developer portal.
configuration.cli:
az servicebus topic create -g rg-app --namespace-name sb-orders -n orders
az servicebus topic subscription create -g rg-app --namespace-name sb-orders --topic-name orders -n billing
az apim create -g rg-api -n apim-contoso --publisher-email api@contoso.com --publisher-name Contoso --sku-name StandardV2

lab.objective: Pick the messaging or eventing service.
expected: Service Bus for enterprise messaging; Event Grid for reactive events; Event Hubs for streams
failureScenarios: Using Event Grid for ordered commands
Using Queue Storage when FIFO and duplicate detection are needed
lab.cost: None. The simulation runs entirely in the browser.

troubleshooting.symptom: Messages are processed twice after retries.
troubleshooting.fix: Make handlers idempotent and enable Service Bus duplicate detection.
Add API Management rate-limit and quota policies.

comparisons.difference: Service Bus: FIFO, transactions, topics, dead-letter; Queue Storage: simple, cheap, huge queues.
Event Grid: discrete events pushed to handlers; Event Hubs: high-volume streams read by consumers.

misconceptions.myth: Events and messages are the same.
misconceptions.reality: A message expects processing; an event announces a fact.

misconceptions.myth: Event Hubs pushes events to subscribers.

architectureDecisions: Messages → Service Bus (or Queue Storage when simple).
Discrete events → Event Grid; streams → Event Hubs.

body: Orders must reach billing and shipping, uploads must trigger processing, devices stream telemetry, and partners call APIs.

steps.label: Messages
steps.title: Commands that must be handled
body: Service Bus: queues and topics with ordering (sessions), duplicate detection and dead-lettering. Topics let each service subscribe with filters. Queue Storage is simpler and cheaper.

steps.label: Events
steps.title: News that something happened
body: Event Grid pushes discrete events (a blob was created) to handlers. Event Hubs ingests millions of events per second as a stream for analytics.

handsOn.title: Publish to a Service Bus topic with filtered subscriptions
handsOn.cost: Low. A Standard namespace is billed hourly (a few US cents for this lab). Delete it the same day.
before: Signed in at portal.azure.com as Owner of a subscription. Work in a resource group called rg-az305-lab.
If rg-az305-lab does not exist yet: Resource groups > Create > name rg-az305-lab, region UAE North (or any region near you) > Review + create > Create.

steps.do: Search 'Service Bus' > Create: rg-az305-lab, unique namespace name, your region, pricing tier Standard.
steps.tip: Basic tier has no topics; topics need Standard or Premium.

steps.do: Open orders > + Subscription: name billing. Create another: shipping.
Open the shipping subscription > Filters: replace the default rule with a SQL filter.
steps.see: Only messages with Country = 'AE' will reach shipping.

steps.do: Open the orders topic > Service Bus Explorer > Send messages: body {"id":1}, add a custom property Country = AE. Send. Send another with Country = US.
Subscriptions > billing > Service Bus Explorer > Peek from start; then shipping.
steps.see: billing has both messages; shipping has only the AE one.
steps.tip: This is publish-subscribe with filters — the sender doesn't know who listens.

check: Each subscription received the messages its filter allows.
cleanup: Resource groups > rg-az305-lab > Delete resource group > type the name > Delete.
